decision: Use duration-bound sampling derived from the benchmark workload duration, and reject explicit intervals whose last sample falls outside the active workload window.

correctness.reason: Every planned sample remains inside the known active DAG duration; the previous 1000ms default would place four of five samples after a 210ms workload.

robustness.winner: fail-closed explicit interval validation plus sample-offset evidence
robustness.reason: Configuration drift cannot silently turn workload calibration into idle calibration, and timing evidence can be checked independently.

performance_resources.winner: derive intervals without extending or repeating the workload
performance_resources.reason: No extra qrexec calls, no daemon, no longer CPU burn, and no change to workload semantics.

regression.winner: standalone sampling policy primitive before CLI integration
regression.reason: Keeps the rule deterministic and unit-testable while minimizing changes to MissionQueue/coordinator code.

rejected.failure: For the canonical 210ms workload, most samples occur after work completes and understate active resource demand.

rejected.approach: repeat or stretch the DAG until all samples finish
rejected.failure: Changes workload semantics and increases CPU/runtime cost, making calibration less representative of the benchmark being sized.

rejected.approach: accept post-workload samples and filter later
rejected.failure: Can leave too few active samples for p95 and hides configuration mistakes instead of failing closed.

qa: 210ms workload with 5 samples derives 52ms interval and last sample at 208ms
1000ms explicit interval for 5 samples is rejected
sample offsets must be monotonic and inside active workload
lesson: Workload lifecycle framing alone is insufficient; resource samples must also be temporally inside the active workload window.
next: Integrate this policy into the real calibration CLI/runtime, emit sampleOffsetMs evidence, and make the collector enforce the timing window before accepting resource samples.
